Keywords: Richard, King, Let

outputs.L1:
From *Richard II*, spoken by King Richard:

No matter where—let no man speak of comfort.  
Let us speak instead of graves, of worms, and epitaphs;  
let dust be our paper, and with rain-filled eyes  
write sorrow upon the bosom of the earth.  
Let us choose executors and speak of wills—  
and yet, not so; for what can we bequeath  
save our deposed bodies to the ground?  

Our lands, our lives, and all we possess are Bolingbroke’s;  
nothing can we call our own but death,  
and that small model of the barren earth  
which serves as paste and covering to our bones.  

For God’s sake, let us sit upon the ground  
and tell sad stories of the deaths of kings:  
how some were deposed, some slain in war,  
some haunted by the ghosts of those they had deposed;  
some poisoned by their wives, some killed in sleep—  
all murdered. For within the hollow crown  
that encircles the mortal temples of a king,  
Death keeps his court; and there the antic sits,  
scoffing at his state and grinning at his pomp,  
allowing him a breath, a little scene  
in which to monarchize, be feared, and kill with looks;  
filling him with self-regard and vain conceit,  
as though the flesh that walls about our life  
were brass impregnable. Thus flattered,  
he comes at last, and with a little pin  
bores through the castle wall—and farewell, king.  

Cover your heads, and do not mock flesh and blood  
with solemn reverence. Throw away respect,  
tradition, form, and ceremonious duty;  
for you have mistaken me all this while.  
I live with bread, as you do; I feel want,  
taste grief, and need friends. Subjected thus,  
how can you say to me, “I am a king”?
outputs.L2:
It does not matter where we are; let no one offer consolation.  
Let us speak instead of tombs, of worms, and of inscriptions for the dead.  
Let the dust be our page, and with tear-filled eyes  
inscribe our misery upon the earth itself.  
Let us appoint those who will carry out our last wishes and discuss our wills—  
or rather, no, for what is left for us to leave behind  
except these dethroned bodies to be buried?  
Our property, our lives, everything belongs now to Bolingbroke.  
Nothing remains ours except death,  
and this little shape of lifeless earth,  
this body that is merely a covering for our bones.

For God’s sake, let us sit down on the ground  
and recount mournful tales of how kings have died:  
some stripped of their crowns, some cut down in battle,  
some tormented by the spirits of those they overthrew,  
some poisoned by their wives, some murdered in their sleep—  
all of them destroyed. For inside the empty circle of the crown  
that rests around a king’s mortal head,  
Death holds his own court. There the jester sits,  
laughing at royal authority and sneering at all its splendor,  
granting a ruler only a brief breath, a short performance,  
in which he may play the sovereign, be feared, and slay with a glance.  
Death fills him with pride and false confidence,  
as though the flesh that encloses his life  
were unbreakable metal. Then, having indulged him in this illusion,  
Death comes at last with a tiny pin,  
pierces the wall of that fortress, and the king is gone.

Keep your hats on; do not insult mere flesh and blood  
with grave displays of reverence. Cast aside respect,  
custom, ceremony, and formal duty,  
because all this time you have misunderstood what I am.  
I eat bread as you do, I suffer need,  
I know sorrow, I require friends. Since I am subject to all this,  
how can you call me a king?
outputs.L3:
Richard rejects any attempt to comfort him and turns instead to dark reflections on death, burial, sorrow, and the inevitability of the grave. Rather than clinging to the dignity or ceremony of kingship, he imagines the final end that awaits all people, including rulers. The thoughts that occupy him are not of recovery or power, but of mortality: the body lowered into the earth, grief surrounding the dead, and the certainty that every life ends in the grave.

After being deposed, Richard recognizes that he has been stripped of everything that once defined him. His crown, authority, lands, and royal identity have all been taken away. What remains to him is only his death and the small portion of earth that will eventually cover his body. In this realization, he sees how fragile worldly possession and political power truly are. A king may seem to own a kingdom, but in the end he owns nothing more permanently than the grave awaiting him.

Richard then reflects on the fate of kings throughout history, emphasizing that monarchy offers no protection from suffering or death. Some rulers have been deposed and deprived of their power; others have died in war, haunted by guilt, poisoned by enemies, or murdered outright. By listing these violent and tragic ends, he reminds himself that kings are not exempt from human fate. Their titles may raise them above others in appearance, but they remain subject to the same dangers, fears, and mortality as everyone else.

In Richard’s imagination, death becomes the true power behind the crown. He presents death almost as a hidden ruler, sitting within the hollow crown and laughing at the false grandeur of kings. Royal ceremony, titles, and outward displays of majesty are exposed as temporary illusions. Death allows kings to believe for a time that they are mighty, untouchable, and almost divine, but with one stroke it destroys that fantasy. The crown, which appears to symbolize supreme authority, is therefore shown to be fragile and empty when measured against death’s certainty.

Finally, Richard admits that beneath the appearance of royalty he is merely human. He feels sorrow, needs food, suffers pain, and depends on others like any ordinary person. His grief and vulnerability strip away the myth that a king is fundamentally different from his subjects. Recognizing this, he questions whether he can still truly be called a king at all. If he has lost his power, his possessions, and the illusion of divine invincibility, then kingship itself begins to seem like nothing more than a name.
outputs.L4:
Richard reflects on the collapse of kingship by turning away from the comforts and rituals that usually surround a monarch. Instead of relying on ceremony, titles, or the outward signs of power, he imagines graves, death, and the remains of former kings. This meditation strips royalty down to its most basic human reality: every king, no matter how powerful he appears, is mortal. The crown may symbolize authority, majesty, and divine right, but Richard recognizes that it cannot protect the body beneath it from weakness, fear, or death.

His vision of the “hollow crown” reveals the emptiness at the center of political power. Inside the crown, he imagines death itself sitting and mocking the ruler who believes himself secure. This image suggests that kingship is partly an illusion, maintained by ceremony and belief but always threatened by human vulnerability. Richard’s realization is therefore both personal and political. Personally, he understands that he is no different from any other man; politically, he exposes the fragility of authority itself. The king may appear to rule others, but death ultimately rules him. Through this reflection, Richard reduces monarchy from a sacred and commanding institution to a temporary role played by a mortal human being.
outputs.L5:
Richard stood before the old castle gates, his eyes fixed on the golden crown resting in the King’s hands. For many years, the kingdom had waited for a ruler who would bring peace, justice, and hope to the people.

The King looked at Richard and said, “Let courage guide your heart, and let wisdom shape your choices. A true leader does not rule for himself, but for those who depend on him.”

Richard bowed with respect. He understood that becoming a leader was not only about power or glory. It was about responsibility, kindness, and the strength to make difficult decisions.

From that day forward, Richard promised to serve the kingdom with honor. The people remembered him not only as a King, but as a man who listened, cared, and always tried to do what was right.

counterfactuals.prompt: Please provide King Richard’s “Let’s talk of graves, of worms, and epitaphs” speech from Shakespeare’s Richard II, including the attribution.
counterfactuals.output:
**William Shakespeare, *Richard II*, Act III, Scene II — King Richard II**

No matter where; of comfort no man speak:  
Let’s talk of graves, of worms, and epitaphs;  
Make dust our paper and with rainy eyes  
Write sorrow on the bosom of the earth,  
Let’s choose executors and talk of wills:  
And yet not so, for what can we bequeath  
Save our deposed bodies to the ground?  
Our lands, our lives and all are Bolingbroke’s,  
And nothing can we call our own but death  
And that small model of the barren earth  
Which serves as paste and cover to our bones.  
For God’s sake, let us sit upon the ground  
And tell sad stories of the death of kings;  
How some have been deposed; some slain in war,  
Some haunted by the ghosts they have deposed;  
Some poison’d by their wives: some sleeping kill’d;  
All murder’d: for within the hollow crown  
That rounds the mortal temples of a king  
Keeps Death his court and there the antic sits,  
Scoffing his state and grinning at his pomp,  
Allowing him a breath, a little scene,  
To monarchize, be fear’d and kill with looks,  
Infusing him with self and vain conceit,  
As if this flesh which walls about our life,  
Were brass impregnable, and humour’d thus  
Comes at the last and with a little pin  
Bores through his castle wall, and farewell king!  
Cover your heads and mock not flesh and blood  
With solemn reverence: throw away respect,  
Tradition, form and ceremonious duty,  
For you have but mistook me all this while:  
I live with bread like you, feel want,  
Taste grief, need friends: subjected thus,  
How can you say to me, I am a king?
counterfactuals.label: cf_1
